section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: The Algebraic Dot Product
section_1.content: Briefly define the dot product as the sum of element-wise products (a · b = Σ a_i b_i). Visualize this as a 'matching' operation: how much do two vectors point in the same direction?
section_1.example: Comparing two grocery lists: Vector A (quantities purchased) vs. Vector B (unit prices). The dot product gives the total cost.

section_2.title: Visualizing Projections
section_2.content: Shift to the geometric definition: a · b = |a||b|cos(θ). Animate vector 'a' casting a shadow onto vector 'b'. Emphasize that the dot product is the length of one vector projected onto another, scaled by the second vector's length.
section_2.example: A hiker pulling a wagon: Only the component of force in the direction of movement contributes to the work done.

section_3.title: The Concept of Duality
section_3.content: Introduce duality: A dot product with a fixed vector 'v' can be viewed as a 'function' (linear map) that turns any input vector 'u' into a scalar. Visualize the fixed vector 'v' as defining a 'level set' of parallel lines (or planes).
section_3.example: A 'Sensor' vector: Imagine a laser grid. A vector passing through the grid triggers a reading based on its alignment with the grid lines; the grid defines the linear function.

section_4.title: Synthesis: The Geometry of Duality
section_4.content: Explain that every linear function (a plane) in space corresponds to a unique vector (its normal). The vector is the 'dual' of the plane. Show an animation where rotating a normal vector perfectly rotates the associated plane.
section_4.example: A 2D character (a robot) trying to detect if an object is 'in front' of its field of view. The robot's 'line of sight' vector is the dual to the boundary line dividing 'safe' from 'danger' zones.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Intuition
section_5.content: Summarize: The dot product is not just math; it is a tool for measuring alignment and projecting points onto boundaries. Duality is the bridge between a 'direction' and the 'slice' it creates.
section_5.example: In machine learning (SVMs), the 'dual' vector defines the decision boundary that classifies cat vs. dog images.
